name: 15i pass at k walkthrough
title: Pass at k counts the chance that k picks include a passing sample
subtitle: Section 2 example: n = 10 samples for one coding problem, c = 3 of them pass the unit tests

steps.caption: We sampled the model 10 times on one problem and ran the unit tests on each answer. Three passed, so c = 3. Pass at k asks how likely a user with k attempts is to get at least one passing answer.
With one attempt the user fails only if the single pick lands on a failure, which happens 7 times in 10. One minus that is 0.30, the plain fraction of passing samples.
With five attempts, failure means all five picks are failures. The outlined set is one of the 21 all-failure sets among 252 possible sets, so pass at 5 is 1 - 21/252, about 0.917.
Plugging 3/10 into 1 - (1 - p)^5 treats the measured 0.3 as exact and gives 0.832. Averaged over many problems that shortcut is biased low, while the counting formula is right on average.
Every budget from 1 to 10 uses the same rule. From k = 8 the value is exactly 1, because 8 picks cannot all come from only 7 failures. The formula needs n at least as large as k.
steps.heading: Same problem, n = 10 and c = 3, pass at k from the counting formula for every budget k

steps.caption: A rare success gains the most from extra attempts: p = 0.1 climbs from 0.10 at k = 1 to 0.88 at k = 20. Pass at 1 and pass at 100 can rank two models differently for that reason.
steps.heading: True pass at k for a per-sample success rate p is $1 - (1 - p)^k$
